History · 18 November 2026

Cajal and the 'butterflies of the soul'

How a doctor from Aragon, drawing at the microscope, showed that the brain is made of separate cells.

At the end of the 19th century, many scientists believed the nervous system was a continuous network, like a mesh of connected tubes. A Spanish doctor, Santiago Ramón y Cajal, spent years at the microscope showing the opposite.

A borrowed and improved method

The Italian Camillo Golgi had invented a silver stain in 1873 that coloured only a few cells in nervous tissue, but did so completely. Cajal came across it in Madrid in 1887, perfected it and applied it mainly to tissue from young animals, in which the cells are seen more clearly.

What he saw convinced him that each neuron is an independent unit, separated from the others by a small gap, and that information flows in one direction. This is the neuron doctrine. Decades later, the electron microscope confirmed that gap, the synapse.

A Nobel shared with his rival

In 1906 Cajal and Golgi jointly received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Golgi used his lecture to defend the network theory and criticise Cajal's. It is one of the oddest cases in the prize's history: two scientists honoured at the same time for work that reached opposite conclusions.

Science and art

Cajal drew what he saw with great precision. His drawings are still used in teaching and have been exhibited in museums around the world. He called the pyramidal neurons of the cortex the "mysterious butterflies of the soul", whose beating wings might one day explain mental life.

His work is still the foundation of neuroscience. When we talk today about brain plasticity or about how connections between neurons change with learning, we are using ideas he had already glimpsed.

References

  1. Ramón y Cajal, S. (1917). Recuerdos de mi vida. Madrid: Imprenta de Juan Pueyo.
  2. DeFelipe, J. (2010). Cajal's butterflies of the soul: Science and art. Nueva York: Oxford University Press.
